body.en: A differential equation relates a function to its rate of change; separable equations integrate directly.
Write \( \tfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y) \) as \( \tfrac{1}{g(y)}\,dy=f(x)\,dx \) and integrate both sides; an initial condition fixes the constant.

Accumulation, Antiderivatives & Differential Flows: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, the accumulation function \(A(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt\) satisfies \(A'(x) = f(x)\), linking instantaneous rates of change to net signed area. In first-order differential equations \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = g(x)h(y)\), separation of variables \(\int \dfrac{1}{h(y)}\,dy = \int g(x)\,dx + C\) reconstructs the family of integral curves across the slope field.

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Differential Equations)

body.en:
Why Integration by Parts & Integrating Factors Work: Differentiating a product \(u(x)v(x)\) gives \((uv)' = u'v + uv'\). Integrating both sides and rearranging yields the Integration by Parts formula:

\[ \int u\,\frac{dv}{dx}\,dx = u v - \int v\,\frac{du}{dx}\,dx \]

Similarly, for a linear first-order ODE \(y' + P(x)y = Q(x)\), multiplying by the integrating factor \(\mu(x) = e^{\int P(x)\,dx}\) (which satisfies \(\mu'(x) = P(x)\mu(x)\)) collapses the left-hand side into an exact product derivative: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\bigl[\mu(x)y\bigr] = \mu(x)Q(x)\).

Problem (Easy): The separable initial value problem \( \dfrac{df}{dx} = 34x \) satisfies \( f(0) = 15 \). Calculate the solution value \( f(3) \).

Step-by-Step Solution: Integrating gives \( f(x) = 17x^2 + 15 \), so \( f(3) = 168 \).

Problem (Medium): The Laplace transform of \( f(x) = 216e^{4x} \) is \( g(s) = \dfrac{216}{s - 4} \) for \( s > 4 \). Calculate the evaluated transform \( g(5) \).

Step-by-Step Solution: Substituting \( s = 5 \) gives \( \frac{216}{5 - 4} = 216 \).

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Differential Equations)

rows.en: Writing \(\ln|y| = x^2 + C \implies y = e^{x^2} + C\)
Exponentiation distributes over addition as multiplication (\(e^{a+b} = e^a e^b\)), not addition.
Write \(y = e^{x^2 + C} = Ae^{x^2}\) and solve for \(A\) using the initial condition.
Leaving original \(x\)-limits on a \(u\)-substituted definite integral
Evaluates the antiderivative \(F(u)\) at \(x\)-values instead of \(u(x)\)-values.
Convert bounds immediately: \(u_{\text{low}} = u(a)\) and \(u_{\text{high}} = u(b)\).
Cancels forward and backward motion (net displacement) instead of accumulating total path length.
Split the integral at every root where \(v(t) = 0\) and integrate \(|v(t)|\).

label.en: ⚠️ Cambridge 9709 Traps — Timing of Constant of Integration & Modulus in Logs

body.en:
Immediate Constant of Integration: The arbitrary constant \(+C\) must be added at the exact line of integration, never tacked on at the end of subsequent algebraic simplification! Integrating \(\int \frac{1}{y}dy = \int k\,dt\) gives \(\ln|y| = kt + C \implies y = e^{kt+C} = Ae^{kt}\). Writing \(\ln y = kt \implies y = e^{kt} + C\) is mathematically invalid and earns zero marks for subsequent work.

Rates of Decay in Word Problems: When formulating a differential equation, words like 'rate of decrease' or 'decay' require an explicit negative sign: \(\frac{dV}{dt} = -k\sqrt{V}\) where \(k > 0\). Omitting the negative turns decay into exponential explosion.

question.en: The temperature \(\theta\) of a cooling metal rod satisfies \(\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -k(\theta - 20)\), where \(t\) is time in minutes and \(k\) is a constant. Given \(\theta = 80\) when \(t = 0\) and \(\theta = 50\) when \(t = 10\), find the value of \(t\) when \(\theta = 30\).

solution.en:
Separate variables and integrate:

\[\int \frac{1}{\theta - 20}\,d\theta = -\int k\,dt \implies \ln(\theta - 20) = -kt + C\]

Apply initial condition \(t = 0, \theta = 80\):

\[\ln(60) = C \implies \ln\left(\frac{\theta - 20}{60}\right) = -kt \implies \theta - 20 = 60e^{-kt}\]

Apply condition \(t = 10, \theta = 50\):

\[30 = 60e^{-10k} \implies e^{-10k} = \frac{1}{2} \implies k = \frac{\ln 2}{10} \approx 0.06931\]

Set \(\theta = 30\):

\[10 = 60e^{-kt} \implies e^{-kt} = \frac{1}{6} \implies t = \frac{\ln 6}{k} = \frac{10\ln 6}{\ln 2} \approx 25.8\text{ minutes}\]

Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: [Practice 3 · Hard] Which differential equation correctly models the statement: "The rate of increase of the volume V of a balloon is proportional to the square of its radius r."?

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Differential Equations and write down the target quantity and domain conditions.
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \( \dfrac{dV}{dt}=kr^2 \).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

solution.en: The correct model is \( \dfrac{dV}{dt}=kr^2 \), where \( k>0 \) is a constant of proportionality. Answer: \(\dfrac{dV}{dt}=kr^2\).
